summary: Defines the operations of SNMPv2 in terms of how messages are sent and received. It covers requests for reading and changing management data and the replies and notifications that come back. It was replaced by RFC 3416.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the messages that SNMPv2 uses to talk to a device. It covers how to ask for a value, how to ask for the next value so you can walk through a table, how to fetch many values at once, how to change a value, and how to announce an event. It also lists the error codes a reply can carry, so that both sides agree on what a failure means.

subtitle: The SNMPv2 request and reply messages: how to read data, change it, and be told when something went wrong.

tldr.problem: SNMPv1 could only fetch one value at a time and had no way to walk a table, so collecting a large amount of management data took many round trips.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines eight PDU types, including GetNext for walking and GetBulk for retrieving many values in one exchange, and it sets out the exact rules for what each one means, including the error codes a response can carry.
tldr.outcome: The bulk request cut the number of exchanges needed to fetch a large table. RFC 1905 was obsoleted by RFC 3416.

facts.label: PDU type codes
facts.value: get 0, get-next 1, response 2, set 3, get-bulk 5, inform 6, trap 7, report 8

sections.title: What SNMPv2 Operations Are
sections.content:
A management system contains several nodes, each with a processing entity, termed an agent, which has access to management instrumentation; at least one management station; and a management protocol used to convey management information between them. The operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework which defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies.

An SNMPv2 entity may act in an agent role, performing management operations in response to received messages other than an inform notification, or when it sends trap notifications. It acts in a manager role when it initiates management operations by generating messages, or when it performs operations in response to a received trap or inform. An entity may support either or both roles, and may also act as a proxy agent, appearing to be in the agent role while satisfying management requests by acting in the manager role with a remote entity.

Three kinds of access to management information are provided. The first is a request-response interaction between a manager and an agent, used to retrieve or modify management information on a managed device. The second is a request-response interaction between two managers, used to notify one manager of information belonging to another. The third is an unconfirmed interaction, in which an agent sends an unsolicited trap to a manager and no response is returned, used to report an exceptional situation that has changed management information.

For all requests, the receiver must under normal circumstances generate and transmit a response to the originator. Whether a request should be retransmitted when no response arrives in time is at the discretion of the application that sent it, and depends on the urgency of the request, but the application must act responsibly about the frequency and duration of retransmissions. The exchange of SNMPv2 messages requires only an unreliable datagram service, with every message entirely and independently contained in a single transport datagram. The preferred mapping is the User Datagram Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMPv2 entities play one or two roles. An agent answers requests about the device it sits on. A manager sends those requests and receives the alerts the agent raises. An entity may play both roles, and may act as a proxy, passing requests on to another device. There are three shapes of exchange: a request and its answer, a notification between two managers that also expects an answer, and an unsolicited alert from an agent that expects none.

sections.title: The PDU Types and Variable Bindings
sections.content:
The management protocol provides for the exchange of messages that convey management information. Each message is a wrapper that encapsulates a Protocol Data Unit. The form and meaning of the wrapper is determined by the administrative framework, which defines the authentication and authorization policies. This document defines the operations with respect to the sending and receiving of the PDUs.

A variable refers to an instance of a non-aggregate object type defined according to the SMI or its textual conventions. A variable binding pairs the name of a variable with its associated value, or, if an exceptional condition occurs during a retrieval request, with an indication of that exception. A variable-binding list is a simple list of variable bindings. The name of a variable is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER formed by concatenating the OBJECT IDENTIFIER of the object type with a fragment identifying the instance; the object type's identifier is called the prefix of the variable.

The PDU types are defined in ASN.1 as a CHOICE: get-request, get-next-request, get-bulk-request, response, set-request, inform-request, snmpV2-trap and report, with the numbers 0, 1, 5, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 8 respectively. The value 4 is obsolete. The report PDU is included, but the RFC notes that its usage and precise semantics are not presently defined and that any administrative framework using it must define them. A PDU carries a request-id, an error-status, an error-index and a variable-bindings list. The bulk PDU, used for get-bulk-request, has the same structure except that the error-status and error-index positions are occupied by non-repeaters and max-repetitions. The upper bound on bindings, called max-bindings, is 2147483647. A variable binding holds a name and either a value or one of three exceptions: unSpecified, noSuchObject and noSuchInstance, plus endOfMibView, which marks the end of the accessible view.
sections.plainLanguage: Every SNMPv2 message carries a protocol data unit, one of eight kinds, each with its own number. A request names the variables it wants by their object identifiers and pairs each name with either a value or one of three exceptions saying why there is no value. The reply repeats the request's identifier so the sender can match it up, and carries an error status and the position of the binding that caused it.

sections.title: Reading: Get, GetNext and GetBulk
sections.content:
The get-request reads named variables. For each binding, if the name exactly matches a variable accessible by the request, the value is set to that variable's value. Otherwise, if the name has no OBJECT IDENTIFIER prefix matching any accessible variable, the value is set to noSuchObject. Otherwise it is set to noSuchInstance. If the response would be larger than the local limit or the originator's maximum message size, an alternate response is generated with error-status tooBig, error-index zero and an empty variable-bindings field; if even that does not fit, the snmpSilentDrops counter is incremented and the message is discarded.

The get-next-request is the basis for walking a table. The receiver locates the variable that is the first lexicographic successor of the requested name among the names accessible by the request, and returns its name and value. If there is no successor, the value field is set to endOfMibView and the name field keeps the requested name. Repeating the request with the name just returned walks through the accessible objects in name order; when the answer is no longer part of the table, the table has been traversed.

The get-bulk-request exists to transfer a potentially large amount of data, including the efficient and rapid retrieval of large tables. Its non-repeaters and max-repetitions fields specify how much is wanted: one binding for each of the first N bindings in the request, and M bindings for each of the remaining R bindings, giving a total of N + (M * R) bindings. Unlike the other request types, a successful bulk request does not map one request binding to one response binding. The response may hold fewer bindings than requested for three reasons: the message would be too large, in which case bindings are removed from the end of the set; every generated binding has the value endOfMibView, in which case the list is truncated after the (N + (i * R))-th binding; or the request needs significantly more processing time than a normal request, in which case an agent may stop early as long as at least one repetition is completed. The RFC also warns that a bulk response can exceed the path MTU, which leads to fragmentation, and that fragmentation is generally considered harmful because it reduces the reliability of the transfer, so under network stress only small values should be used for max-repetitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Get asks for named values. GetNext asks for whatever comes next in name order, so repeating it walks through a table row by row until the answer stops belonging to the table. GetBulk asks for a whole batch at once, and the request says how many single values and how many repeated values it wants. The reply may contain fewer values than asked for, and the RFC lists the three reasons that is allowed.

sections.title: Writing with Set and the Error Codes
sections.content:
The set-request changes values, and it is processed as a two phase operation. In the first phase every binding is validated; only if all the validations succeed does the second phase begin, in which each variable is altered. Implementors may split either phase into several implementation phases, and the RFC says such splits may be needed to ensure consistency.

The validations run in order until one fails, and the first failure sets the error-status and the error-index to the position of the failed binding. The order is: noAccess when the name would be denied because it is not in the appropriate MIB view; notWritable when no variable sharing the same prefix can be created or modified; wrongType when the value's ASN.1 type does not match what the prefix requires; wrongLength when the length does not match; wrongEncoding when the encoding does not match the field's ASN.1 tag; wrongValue when the value could under no circumstances be assigned; noCreation when the name does not exist and could never be created; inconsistentName when the name does not exist but cannot be created under present circumstances; notWritable again when the variable exists but cannot be modified whatever the new value; inconsistentValue when the value could be held under other circumstances but not now; resourceUnavailable when the assignment needs a resource that is unavailable; and genErr for any other failure.

When all validations succeed, error-status is noError and error-index is zero, and the named variables are created if necessary and the specified values assigned, each as if simultaneously with the others. If the same variable is named more than once with different values, the actual assignment is implementation-specific. If any assignment fails, all the others are undone and the error-status becomes commitFailed; if it is not possible to undo all the assignments, it becomes undoFailed with error-index zero. The RFC says implementations are strongly encouraged to avoid both codes.

The error-status values run from noError(0) to inconsistentName(18). A manager must be able to handle a response carrying noSuchName, badValue or readOnly. When the error-status is non-zero the value fields in the bindings are ignored, and a non-zero error-index identifies which binding caused the failure, counting from one.
sections.plainLanguage: A write is checked before anything is changed. Every binding is tested in a fixed order, and the first failure stops the write and tells the sender which binding was at fault. Only when every binding passes are the values assigned, and if one assignment then fails, the RFC asks for the others to be undone. The reply carries an error code and the position of the binding that failed, so both sides agree on what went wrong.

sections.title: Traps and Informs
sections.content:
The SNMPv2-trap is generated by an entity in the agent role when an exceptional situation occurs. The destinations are chosen in an implementation-dependent fashion. The first two bindings in the list are always sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0. If the OBJECTS clause is present in the invocation of the corresponding NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro, each corresponding variable is copied in order into the variable-bindings field, and any additional variables the generating entity chooses to include are copied in as well. No response is returned to a trap.

The inform-request is generated by an application in an entity in the manager role that wants to notify another application, in an entity also in the manager role, of information in a MIB view that is remote to the receiving application. The destinations are specified by the requesting application, and the first two bindings are again sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0. On receipt, the receiving entity checks whether the response would exceed the local limit or the originator's maximum message size; if it would, an alternate response with error-status tooBig and an empty variable-bindings field is sent and processing stops. Otherwise it presents the contents to the appropriate application, generates a response with the same request-id and bindings and error-status noError, and transmits it to the originator.
sections.plainLanguage: A trap is a one-way alert from a device, sent when something exceptional happens, and it asks for nothing in return. An inform is a message between two managers that does expect an answer, so the sender knows the notification arrived. Both carry the same first two entries: how long the device has been up, and the identifier of the notification.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states in one sentence that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document is about the operations of the protocol, and the protection of those operations is the job of the administrative framework, which is what defines the authentication and authorization policies for the message wrapper.
sections.plainLanguage: This document says nothing about security. It defines what the messages mean, while the administrative framework, which wraps each message, is what decides who is allowed to send them and how they are checked.

viz.caption: THE SNMPv2 PDU TYPES AND THEIR NUMBERS

items.label: get-request
items.desc: Read the value of named variables.

items.label: get-next-request
items.desc: Return the next variable in name order, which is how a table is walked.

items.label: response
items.desc: The answer to a request.

items.label: set-request
items.desc: Change the value of named variables.

items.label: get-bulk-request
items.desc: Read a large amount of data, such as a whole table, in one exchange.

items.label: inform-request
items.desc: Tell another manager, and expect an answer.

items.label: snmpV2-trap
items.desc: An unsolicited alert from an agent, with no answer.

items.label: report
items.desc: The RFC does not define the usage or semantics of this PDU.

viz.caption: THE ERROR STATUS CODES AND WHAT THEY MEAN

items.label: noError
items.desc: The request succeeded.

items.label: tooBig
items.desc: The response would be larger than the maximum message size.

items.label: noSuchName
items.desc: The named object does not exist.

items.label: badValue
items.desc: The value is not correct for the object.

items.label: readOnly
items.desc: The object cannot be written.

items.label: genErr
items.desc: A general error.

items.label: noAccess
items.desc: The object is outside the MIB view for this request.

items.label: wrongType
items.desc: The value has the wrong ASN.1 type.

items.label: wrongLength
items.desc: The value has the wrong length.

items.label: wrongEncoding
items.desc: The value is not encoded for the field's ASN.1 tag.

items.label: wrongValue
items.desc: The value could under no circumstances be assigned to the object.

items.label: noCreation
items.desc: The object does not exist and could not ever be created.

items.label: inconsistentValue
items.desc: The value cannot be assigned under the present circumstances.

items.label: resourceUnavailable
items.desc: A resource needed for the assignment is unavailable.

items.label: commitFailed
items.desc: An assignment failed, so the other assignments were undone.

items.label: undoFailed
items.desc: An assignment failed and could not be undone.

items.label: authorizationError
items.desc: The request was not authorized.

items.label: notWritable
items.desc: The object cannot be created or modified.

items.label: inconsistentName
items.desc: The object cannot be created under the present circumstances.
